hints: Start from the parents described. What are the genotypes of the double homozygous dominant parent and the double homozygous recessive parent, and what genotype must all the F1 therefore receive?
Think about what gametes the F1 plants can make when the two genes are on different autosomes. How does independent assortment shape the combinations of A/a and B/b?
Recall the rule given for the phenotype. If either A or B alone is enough for awns, which single F2 genotype will lack awns?
Remember a full genetic diagram needs parental genotypes, gametes, a Punnett square with F2 genotypes, and phenotypes linked to those genotypes.
Count how many of the 16 Punnett boxes contain at least one dominant allele versus how many are fully recessive to get the F2 phenotypic ratio.
walkthrough:
Work out the F1 genotype**
The parents are AABB x aabb, so every F1 gets AB from one parent and ab from the other. All F1 are AaBb and all have awns, which fits because they carry both dominant alleles.

Set up the F2 cross**
The F2 is made by crossing F1 x F1: AaBb x AaBb. Because the genes are on different autosomes they assort independently, so each parent makes four gamete types in equal proportion: $AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$.

Fill the Punnett square and assign phenotypes**
Draw a 4x4 square with those gametes on each side to give 16 combinations. Use the rule that presence of either A or B gives awns. That means AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb, AAbb, Aabb, aaBB, aaBb all have awns. Only the double recessive aabb has no awns.

State the ratio**
15 boxes out of 16 contain at least one A or one B, and 1 box out of 16 is aabb. So the F2 phenotypic ratio is $15$ awn : $1$ no awn.

Final answer: F1: AaBb x AaBb. Gametes: AB, Ab, aB, ab x AB, Ab, aB, ab. F2 genotypes in 4x4 Punnett square with phenotypes: all genotypes with A- or B- have awns, only aabb has no awns. F2 phenotypic ratio: 15 awn : 1 no awn.

hints: Look at your 15:1 ratio and ask why it is a modified form of the normal 9:3:3:1 dihybrid ratio where one phenotype dominates.
walkthrough:
Link the ratio to the interaction**
A normal dihybrid with no interaction gives 9:3:3:1. Here 9+3+3 are all collapsed into one awn phenotype because A masks the absence of B and B masks the absence of A. When either dominant allele alone produces the same phenotype, this is called duplicate dominant epistasis, and because the genes are on autosomes it is autosomal dominant inheritance.
Final answer: duplicate dominant epistasis (autosomal dominant, dihybrid inheritance).

hints: Look at Fig. 3.1 - the awn is a long pointed projection. How could such a structure help a wild seed move, attach, feed or avoid being eaten?
walkthrough:
Connect structure to survival in the wild**
In the wild no farmer sows the seed, so the plant must disperse and establish its own offspring. A long bristle can catch on animal fur for dispersal, help the grain dig into or anchor in soil, deter feeding, or help trap water and nutrients. Any one valid survival benefit explains why awned plants are common in wild rice.
Final answer: awns aid seed dispersal / attach to animals / help anchor grain in soil / deter predators / aid water and nutrient uptake.

hints: Think about who is the selection pressure here compared with natural selection in the wild.
If farmers want no awns and higher yield, which plants in a variable field would they choose to keep seed from?
What must farmers do with those chosen plants to pass on the desired alleles to the next generation?
Consider why one round of choosing is not enough to fix the trait in the whole crop.
walkthrough:
Humans replace natural selection**
This is artificial selection, also called selective breeding. Farmers act as the selection pressure because they decide which phenotype survives to reproduce.

Select and breed the best**
Farmers identify variation, then select plants or seeds showing the desired trait, grains with no awns. They breed those selected plants together, for example by interbreeding them or allowing self-pollination, and collect the seed.

Repeat over generations**
The seeds are germinated and grown, the offspring that still show no awns are again selected and bred. Repeating this cycle over many generations increases the frequency of the recessive a and b alleles until the crop reliably produces grains with no awns.

Final answer: artificial selection by humans; select plants / seeds with no awns; breed / interbreed or self-pollinate selected plants; grow offspring from seed; repeat selection and breeding over many generations until no-awn phenotype is fixed.

hints: Start with the DNA change at the An-1 locus and what that means for the protein product made from that gene.
Think about how a changed primary structure alters the 3D shape of a transcription factor and its ability to bind DNA at the promoter.
Use the two bullet points about positive regulation of awn genes and negative regulation of grain-number genes to predict the opposite effect when the factor is missing.
walkthrough:
From mutation to faulty transcription factor**
A mutation changes the base sequence of An-1, so the coded transcription factor has a different amino acid sequence and therefore a different primary and tertiary structure. The faulty factor is not produced correctly or cannot bind to the promoter / DNA of its target genes.

Loss of positive regulation removes awns**
Normally the factor increases expression of genes for awn development. Without functional binding, transcription of those genes decreases, so awns do not develop.

Loss of negative regulation increases yield**
Normally the same factor decreases expression of genes for grain number. Without functional binding, that repression is lost, so expression of grain-number genes increases and more grains are produced.

Final answer: mutation / change in base sequence of An-1 so transcription factor has altered / non-functional shape and cannot bind promoter; loss of positive regulation so decreased expression of awn development genes giving no awns; loss of negative regulation so increased expression of grain-number genes giving increased yield.
